Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: At sixty-six, Aroha, a woman of Oceania heritage, had built a quiet life running her boutique after her divorce, but the afternoon bled into evening when the sky bruised purple at precisely 8:15 p.m. and the unmarked sedan pulled up behind her. The officer’s commands were sharp, his baton cracking against her shoulder before she could explain she was merely locking the door. When the second cruiser arrived, the flashing lights fractured the dusk, and Aroha felt the world tilt violently during the police violence. She could not recall how she ended up pressed against the wet pavement, nor the sequence of shouts that followed; the official report would later call it a tactical restraint, but Aroha’s mind simply erased those minutes. The experience felt like a scene from someone else’s life, too extreme to be hers, and when she tried to describe the weight of the officer’s knee or the smell of his boots, the words would not come. Now, as the clock in her shop ticks toward eight, the familiar dizziness washes over her, and the empty aisles suddenly feel thick with the eyes of strangers. Over the months that followed, the immediate physical alarm and the sensation of being observed directly fueled her retreat into avoidance and impulse buying, while the same cues forced the memory into disjointed, unplaceable fragments. When the evening light faded, the sensory overload convinced her that she is fundamentally inadequate, unable to manage the basic responsibilities of running a business or a household. To numb the tightness in her chest, she began scrolling through online catalogs, purchasing expensive handcrafted soaps and silk scarves she had no use for, while the calendar on her wall marked the upcoming anniversary with a red pen she refused to use. Her small storefront, once a source of pride, now felt like a trap where the floorboards creaked with threatening familiarity, driving her to bolt the front door early and retreat to the back room. Because she judged herself a poor coper for this fragmentation, Aroha stopped trusting her own recollection, causing the missing pieces to feel even more ominous and the unreal quality of the memory to solidify into a permanent block. She was certain that her spiraling behavior signaled she was losing her grip on reality, and that very fear stripped the remaining fragments of any therapeutic value, leaving her with only the raw, wordless terror of that night. Conversely, the memory’s unresolved nature only made the sensation of being watched more potent when the clock struck eight, while the compulsion to spend and the habit of isolation only made the dizziness more severe upon her return to the storefront. The memory’s persistent gaps and unreal quality drove her to seal herself away from the evening light and stockpile distractions, as the disjointed trauma demanded a permanent retreat. Hiding in the back room and avoiding the anniversary week only starved her mind of the chance to integrate the trauma, ensuring the memory remained fractured and unplaceable. The very act of wrapping herself in purchased comforts to outrun the memory only deepened her belief that she was a lousy coper, as the avoidance proved she could not face her own life. The raw, wordless terror of that night only reinforced her conviction that she was fundamentally inadequate, as the disjointed trauma demanded a permanent retreat. Aroha finally walked into the clinic because her PCL-5 score of seventy-eight reflected the crushing weight of these symptoms, and the compulsion to spend was draining her retirement savings; she is most terrified that she will never feel safe in her own neighborhood again, and she is desperately hoping to find a way to remember the truth without feeling like she is drowning.
